story:
Hazel's little brother, Gus, had one mission at the science museum: find the ice cream machine before their parents finished the space exhibit. Hazel had a different mission: beat the "Matter Mixer" quiz at the back of the chemistry hall, which nobody in her class had ever beaten without missing a question. The prize was a sticker that read MOLECULE BOSS, and she wanted it stuck to her binder by lunch.

The hall smelled faintly like pennies. Near the entrance, a display called the tundra table held a tray of ice cubes under a warm lamp, slowly slumping into puddles. Beside it stood a chunk of iron fence, speckled orange and crumbling, with a sign that said it had come from a dilapidated lighthouse up the coast. Farther along, a sealed case let visitors press a button and watch a strip of magnesium flare into blinding white powder, then cool into ash. Hazel pressed it three times, partly for science and partly because it was spectacular.

The quiz machine flashed its first question: Ice cubes melt in the sun. Did anything new get made? Hazel stared at the puddle tray. She crouched, dipped a finger in, and touched it to her tongue. Water. Just water, the same stuff as ice, only sloshier. "So that's a physical change," she muttered. "The shape changed, but the substance didn't." Then she looked at the rusted fence, flaking orange under the lights, and the ash in the case. Those were different. If she scraped the rust off, it wouldn't be iron anymore; if she tried to burn the powder back together, it would just laugh at her. Something new had been made there. She answered: nothing new. The machine chimed.

Gus appeared at her elbow, breathing hard. "No ice cream machine," he reported grimly. "But there's a slushie stand, and slushie is basically ice plus syrup, so technically I'm still on mission." Hazel answered six more questions, missing only the one about burned toast, and the machine spat out her sticker. She slapped it on her binder, then held it up so the lamp light could expose its glittery gold letters. "Say it," she told Gus. He sighed like a man on the tundra surrendering his last sandwich. "Hail the Molecule Boss." She handed him a napkin for the slushie he was already planning.

activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
story:
Emilie stood on the coffee table in the living room, holding a note card so tightly it bent. Her little brother Theo sat on the couch with a stopwatch, because Theo wanted to be a race announcer when he grew up, and he considered timing things his official job. "Speech is Friday," Emilie said. "Two minutes, and Miss Okafor is strict about it." Her best point, the story of Grandpa's old propeller plane and the day he landed it on a frozen lake, was buried in the middle, but she didn't know that yet.

She gave the speech to Theo. She opened with a boring question, "Have you ever wondered about aviation?", then talked about three points, then closed with a shrug and the word "anyway." Theo clicked the stopwatch and frowned. "Two minutes and six seconds," he announced. "But Emilie, what was your speech about?" She told him again. "No, what you said. I remember the question at the start and 'anyway' at the end, and the rest is just... fog."

Emilie sat down on the rug. Theo looked lethargic, slumped sideways like the speech had drained the energy right out of him, and that gave her an idea. She needed to isolate the problem, so she gave the speech one more time, exactly the same, except this time she started with the propeller plane story and ended with it too. Theo sat up straight. When she finished, he could name all three points in order. "The middle one I only sort of remember," he admitted, "but the first and last, those are stuck in my head." Emilie grabbed her note cards. "Then that's where the good stuff goes. Miss Okafor said people remember the first and last items in a list best. It's called the serial position effect." Theo repeated the words slowly, like a race announcer saying a new driver's name. "Serial position effect. Sounds fast."

On Friday morning Emilie practiced one last time in the living room, opening with the frozen lake and closing with the propeller spinning in the cold air. Theo clicked the stopwatch at exactly two minutes and raised both arms. "And the winner, by the power of the serial position effect, is Emilie!" She laughed, gathered her note cards, and walked out the front door with her chin up.

activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
story:
Christopher sat on the back step with his sketchbook, a golf ball, and a flashlight propped against a flowerpot. His assignment was to draw the ball so it looked round instead of like a flat white circle, and so far he had four flat white circles to prove how hard that was.

His little sister Nadia wandered over, licking a popsicle. "That's a nice cookie," she said, pointing at his latest attempt.

"It's a sphere," Christopher groaned. "It's supposed to look three-dimensional."

"Then why doesn't it?"

He tapped his pencil against his chin. Maybe the problem was that he had shaded everything the same gray, like the ball was made of the same stuff all the way around, which it was, but that wasn't the point. He looked at the real golf ball under the flashlight. One side of it gleamed. Not all of it, just one small bright spot, sitting on the side that faced the light.

Nadia leaned in and squinted at his drawing. "Which side is the lamp on?"

Christopher opened his mouth to answer and then stopped. He couldn't answer. In his drawing there was no side facing the light, because he hadn't put a brightest spot anywhere. He grabbed his eraser and rubbed out his careful gray wash until the paper looked rough and porous, like a worn-out kitchen sponge.

"That's backwards," Nadia said. "You're erasing your homework."

"I'm eliminating the flatness," said Christopher. "Watch."

He studied the golf ball again. The brightest spot sat right where the ball faced the flashlight, so he made one small bright patch on the upper right of his sphere and left it almost untouched, then let the shading grow darker toward the far side, until the shadow the ball threw onto the flowerpot behind it made a long dark tail.

"Which side is the lamp on now?" he asked.

Nadia pointed at the bright patch without hesitating. "That side. It's like the ball is telling on the flashlight."

Christopher held the drawing up next to the real thing and grinned. "A snitching sphere."

"Draw a face on it," Nadia said, "and make the face look guilty."

He laughed and turned the page, already sketching a lumpy, sneaky-looking ball with the highlight gleaming on its shining, tattletale side.

activity: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
story:
Dominic had been rehearsing his speech the whole bus ride to the town hall, and by the time he pushed through the big wooden doors, he could say "petition" without tripping over it even once. He wanted the town to change the bylaw that banned skateboards in Riverside Park, and tonight he was going to tell them so. He clutched his petition, forty-two signatures in blue and green ink, plus one in purple crayon from his little sister, who had signed it "Trixie, age six, skateboarder at heart."

The meeting room smelled like coffee and old carpet. Dominic found a seat near the front, next to Councillor Ruiz, who had once helped him rescue a kite from a tree. "Perfect timing," she whispered. "Public petitions come first on the agenda."

Dominic marched to the microphone. He explained that skateboarders were getting chased to the parking lot, which was honestly more dangerous, and that a park should be versatile enough for soccer players and skateboarders both. He held up his pages of signatures like a trophy. The room clapped, and one man in a flannel shirt called out, "The kid's got stamina! I gave up on petitions years ago!"

Councillor Ruiz stood up, and Dominic grinned. She was going to fix it right now. "Thank you, Dominic," she said. "I'd love to change this bylaw myself, but I can't. A single councillor can't change a bylaw alone. It needs a majority vote of the whole council."

Dominic felt like a goalie who had just watched the ball sail past him. Then he thought about it. Majority. He counted the councillors at the long table, eight of them, plus Councillor Ruiz. A rule nobody could see was standing between him and the park, and rules like that had to be moved a different way, not by one friendly grown-up but by enough votes stacked together. He had one signature on the council, sort of. He needed five.

So during the break he went to work. He walked the whole table, showing each councillor his purple crayon signature, asking if they had questions, offering to collaborate on a plan for a skate corner with a fence so soccer balls wouldn't get flattened. Councillor Okafor, who looked grumpy all night, actually laughed. "You've done more homework than most adults who show up here," she said.

When the vote came, Dominic sat on his hands to keep from drumming the armrest. The clerk read the names one by one. Yes. Yes. No. Yes. Yes. Yes. Councillor Okafor paused, looked straight at Dominic, and said, "Yes, for the crayon signature alone."

The gavel came down, and the whole room turned toward him. Dominic raised both fists in the air, and Trixie's purple crayon, held high like a torch, caught the light.

story:
Mason wanted the last spot on the science demonstration team more than he wanted lunch, and lunch at his school was actually pretty good. The tryout was simple: bring a change, show it, and say whether it was physical or chemical. Priya, who sat in front of him, wanted the spot too, and she had brought a tray with an ice cube melting on it, plus her older brother's good flashlight. Her cube was already shrinking under the lamp, and she looked calm, which made Mason's stomach tighten.

He had planned to burn a strip of paper, but Coach Reyes had banned matches, so all he had was his grandfather's old letter about last summer's campfire, folded in his pocket like a secret weapon. He read it to the class.

"Dear Mason. You asked me why I couldn't save the burnt logs for next year, the way we froze the leftover lemonade. Here is what happened. The wood combined with oxygen in the air and turned into ash, carbon dioxide, and water vapour. The smoke you watched drift up was some of those gases going away. You cannot scoop them back and remake the logs. That's the whole answer. Grandpa."

A boy in the back raised his hand. "But my ice pop melts and I refreeze it all the time."

"That's the difference," Mason said. "Melting is physical. The ice is still water, just loose. Refreeze it and it's ice again. Burning is a chemical change. The wood turns into new stuff. Those three things. And it can't turn back into wood, ever."

Priya touched her melting cube, then looked at her tray in a new way, almost disappointed, as if her clever trick had shrunk to something small. But she had no resentment; she scribbled a note and slid it across. "Ash, carbon dioxide, AND water vapour? I only said physical. You got it." Mason wrote back one word: "Team?" She underlined it twice and added a smile.

Coach Reyes walked over carrying the scorched pan from the supply closet. "Somebody burned popcorn in this last year. Explain it."

Mason grinned. "The kernels combined with oxygen. The pan can transport the evidence to the trash, but nothing will turn it back into popcorn." Then he paused. "Could we weigh ash before and after, to see where the rest went?"

activity: to search the web with specific keywords and tell an ad from a real result
story:
Charlotte was supposed to be helping Mom distribute flyers for the neighborhood cleanup, but she had stopped at the coffee table, pencil tapping her chin. A song was stuck in her head, three words of it, and she could not remember the rest. She had tried humming it to her little brother, who just laughed, and now she was staring at her mom's laptop like it might blink first.

She typed purple October cat and pressed enter. The results were useless. A pet store, a Halloween costume, an eccentric artist who painted everything violet. Then she remembered something her cousin had said last summer, messing around on the computer: "Put quotes around it and it has to match." At the time Charlotte had shrugged and gone back to her popsicle. That had been a mistake, she decided now. She should have paid attention.

She typed "purple October cat" with the quotation marks around the phrase, all three words inside them, exactly as she remembered them. The page changed. Every result now contained those exact words in that exact order, and the fourth one down was the song. She clicked it, and the missing words came flooding back with the tune. On the TV in the corner, a courtroom show droned on, a defendant in a wrinkled suit insisting he had returned the ladder.

Then something else caught her eye. At the top of her results sat a shiny box that said Ad in tiny gray letters, promising purple cat sweaters for October. She looked at it, then at the plain results below. So that was the trick. The real answers looked boring, and the fancy box just wanted her money. She thought about how many times she had clicked the fancy box before, without ever noticing the tiny gray word.

She pulled a flyer from the stack to show Mom, then typed one more search, in quotes, just to watch the list snap into order. "You found the song?" Mom called from the kitchen. "Third result," Charlotte said. "The real one, not the ad."

activity: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
story:
Grandpa's laptop sat on the kitchen table between a plate of peanut butter toast and a glass prism that caught the morning light and threw little rainbows across the wall. Alice had claimed the laptop the moment she arrived, because today she was going to finish her Scratch game, the one where a cat trotted around a garden collecting golden coins.

She dragged a coin onto the stage, then clicked the cat and built her script. "When the green flag is clicked, move with the arrow keys, and if touching the coin, change score by one," she muttered, reading her blocks out loud like a spell. She clicked the flag and steered the cat straight over the coin with her agile fingers on the arrow keys. The score stayed at zero.

"That coin is being stubborn," said Grandpa, leaning over her shoulder with his toast. "Try again." Alice circled the cat around the coin, then back over it. Still zero. She frowned and clicked the flag again, and this time she watched very carefully as the cat crossed the coin. Nothing happened. No pop, no point, nothing.

The problem had to be invisible, somewhere in the blocks themselves, and that gave her a funny feeling. It reminded her of last summer, when the porch light flickered every night and Grandpa blamed moths until Alice stood out there for ten whole minutes and discovered it was a loose bulb, twisting in the wind. You couldn't see the cause; you had to hunt for it. "Same thing," she told herself. "The bug is hiding in the script."

She read her blocks again, one at a time, like a detective. The "if touching coin" block sat there at the bottom, all by itself, outside everything. Maybe, she thought, it only got one chance to check, right when the script started, and after that it went to sleep. So she tried something. She found the "forever" block, dropped it around her movement blocks, and tucked the "if touching" block inside the forever loop. Then the cat would cross the coin, and the check would happen again and again, over and over, instead of just once.

She clicked the green flag and steered the cat onto the coin. The score jumped to one. "Grandpa! It works!" She bounced the cat around the garden like a small moon in orbit, collecting coin after coin, watching the number climb: two, five, nine. Grandpa tapped the screen. "Eleven coins? I demand a rematch after lunch." Alice grinned and hit the green flag one more time.

activity: to revise a draft by cutting weak adjectives and varying sentence length
story:
Rachel read her race scene aloud to the writing club and watched Marcus's face go politely blank. The paragraph described Tessa "running very quickly down the very steep hill, her heart beating really fast." It was supposed to feel breathless. Instead it sounded like a grocery list.

"Read it again," said Priya, tapping the table, "but this time cross out every word like very and really before you start." Rachel scanned the page. There were eleven of them. She drew a line through each one, and when she read the scene a second time, something odd happened: it got faster, not weaker. She frowned at the page as if it had tricked her.

Then she came to the part where Tella "ran very quickly" toward the finish line, and the whole race still felt slow. She stared at the two words, ran and quickly, and thought about her track meet in September, when she had hung back too long on the final curve. What had she actually done in that last stretch? She had sprinted. Rachel crossed out three words and wrote one. "Sprinted," she said out loud. "It says more than ran very quickly." Marcus sat up. Priya grabbed her own draft and started hunting through it like each verb was a candidate for firing, which, Rachel realized, was exactly what they were.

She broke her long sentences apart too. Short line. Then a longer one that gathered speed and carried the reader down the hill without stopping. Priya's pencil hovered over her page. "My narrator's mood is volatile in chapter two," she said. "One minute calm, the next furious. Think I should do this there?" Rachel looked at her own before-and-after pages, unsure which version a stranger would believe was written by someone who had actually run a race. "Try it," she said. "Read both out loud. If the angry one still sounds calm, cut harder." Priya flipped to chapter two and began reading, and the room went quiet except for pencils.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
story:
In the market square in Sevilla, Arianna clutched her notebook and tried to remember why she had ever agreed to speak only Spanish for a whole day. Her older brother, Marco, had promised her ten euros if she could describe the entire family to their host, Señora Reyes, using full sentences before sunset. Ten euros was real income for a twelve-year-old with her eye on a leather journal in the shop by the cathedral, so she marched up to the kitchen table, sat down, and opened her notebook to the page of sentences she had written on the plane.

"Mi hermano Marco es alto," she began, pointing at Marco, who was leaning in the doorway looking smug. "Mi madre es simpática. Mi padre es muy alto también." Señora Reyes nodded along, smiling, and then asked the question Arianna had been dreading. "¿Tienes mascotas?" Arianna did have pets, two of them, and she flipped to her notes. She had written "un negro gato" for Midnight and "una blanca perra" for Pepper, because that was how you said it in English, black cat, white dog. She read the words out loud, and Señora Reyes tilted her head the way people do when something sounds wrong but they are too polite to say so.

Arianna's face went hot, but she refused to give up ten euros to embarrassment. She thought about the signs she had seen all morning, the bakery with "pan fresco" painted on its window, the stall selling "naranjas dulces." The describing word came second, every single time, like a rule hiding in plain sight. That had to imply something about her own sentences, so she tested it right there at the table. "Un gato negro," she said slowly, watching Señora Reyes's face, "y una perra blanca."

"¡Perfecto!" Señora Reyes clapped her hands. "Un gato negro," she repeated, and Marco, who had wandered over pretending to be indifferent, actually wrote it on his own hand.

By sunset Arianna had earned her ten euros, describing every cousin, every aunt, and even the neighbor's indifferent orange cat, and she marched straight to the shop by the cathedral. "Quiero el cuaderno negro," she told the shopkeeper, and when he handed her the exact right one, she grinned all the way to the door.

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
story:
Emily sat on the fence rail at her grandfather's farm, a blank page on her clipboard, trying to formulate her science homework into something she could actually draw: a food chain that started with the sun and ended with a top predator. Sun, grass, grasshopper, frog, snake, hawk. That part was easy. The hard part was the second question: what happens when one link disappears?

She kept thinking about the science museum in town, the trip her class had taken last spring. There had been a big arch of wooden blocks, and a boy named Danny had pulled out the middle top stone. The whole arch had come down, blocks clattering everywhere, even though that one stone looked exactly like all the others. Emily had written about it in a postcard to her friend Rosa, and she dug it out of her pocket now, reading her own words again: "Danny pulled one stone and the arch fell. The guide said that stone was the keystone. One block, whole arch down."

She looked out at the hay field. A hawk circled low, then dove. "Grandpa," she called down the hill, "what if all the snakes around here disappeared? They're not that many." Her grandfather leaned on his rake and considered it. "Snakes eat frogs," he said. "Frogs eat grasshoppers."

Emily drew arrows in her mind. No snakes meant more frogs at first, then fewer grasshoppers, then the grass would grow unchecked, and the hawks that hunted snakes would go hungry or leave. The whole field could change from one missing link. It was like the arch, except the arch was blocks you could see, and this was a pattern you had to reason out. She could not watch it happen directly, but she could test the idea on paper, pulling one link out of her chain and following the arrows one at a time.

She wrote her answer: a species whose removal changes its whole community far more than its numbers would suggest is called a keystone species, and her example was the snake. Then, to keep herself objective, she tried removing the grasshopper instead, and the chain barely wobbled, because grasshoppers were numerous enough that the frogs would find other insects. Danny's stone had taught her something after all. She slid off the fence and ran down the hill to show her grandfather the page, waving it over her head.

"Look, it's the arch," she said.

activity: to recognise the warning signs of anxiety in a friend and know who to tell
story:
Emily noticed it the way you notice a drip behind a wall: not all at once, but once you heard it, you couldn't stop. Maya, who used to demolish a whole slice of pizza at lunch and talk the whole time, now picked at crusts and said almost nothing. She'd stopped coming to Emily's house after school, too, and her texts had gone from long messages to one word: "busy." Emily kept a note in her binder and wrote down what she saw, dates and everything, because her mom called that kind of note-taking an analysis and said it helped you see patterns you'd otherwise miss.

The pattern was ugly. Maya's hands shook when the teacher called on her. She went to the bathroom three times during one math class. On Thursday, she left her lunch untouched and spent recess standing alone by the fence, staring at the field like it was a mile of open water she'd been told to swim.

Emily had a theory, and she knew it was a naive one, the kind you'd be embarrassed to say out loud: maybe Maya was just tired. But tired didn't explain the fence, or the shaking, or the "busy." So she decided to test it. She wrote a note and slipped it into Maya's locker, because Maya wouldn't look at anyone long enough to talk.

The note said: "You don't have to answer this. But if something's wrong, I won't tell the whole grade. I'd only tell one grown-up, and only if you said it was okay. Is something wrong? Circle yes or no."

On Friday morning Emily checked the locker slot between classes, her heart going like a drumroll. The note was there, folded into a tight square. Inside, in Maya's careful handwriting, a "yes" was circled so hard the pencil had torn the paper. Underneath: "I can't stop thinking bad stuff is going to happen. My cousin had this. He got help. Can you come over?"

They sat on Emily's porch after school, the wood warm and smelling like summer even though it was October, a jar of lemonade sweating between them. "My cousin sees a counselor," Maya said. "It's called cognitive behavioral therapy. It teaches you to notice the anxious thoughts and change them. He says it's one of the most effective treatments, and it works, because anxiety disorders are treatable." She took a breath. "I want that. But I'm scared to tell my mom."

"You wrote me a note because talking felt too big," Emily said. "So we'll do it smaller." She slid her binder across the porch, open to the page of dates and observations. "Show her this. You don't have to say anything first. She can read."

Maya's mom read it that evening, standing in the kitchen with flour still on her hands. When she finished, she sat down, pulled Maya's chair closer, and picked up the phone.

"Mrs. Alvarez, hi. I'd like to ask about scheduling an appointment."

story:
Naomi sat on the fence rail outside the barn with her science homework flattened against her knees. Sun, grass, grasshopper, frog, hawk: she was supposed to draw a food chain from the sun all the way up to a top predator, then explain what would happen if one link disappeared. She had the drawing part done. The second part made her stop. Would one missing link really change anything? Her cousin Theo, who was splitting wood nearby, was skeptical too. "It's a big farm," he said, resting the axe against the stump. "Take away one kind of bug and everything else just shrugs."

Naomi thought about the tide pools she had visited last summer on the Washington coast, and about the ranger there, an old man who had leaned on his walking stick and told them about a scientist named Robert Paine. "He took the starfish off a stretch of this shore," the ranger had said. "The starfish eat mussels. After that, the mussels took over the rocks and crowded out many other species." Naomi had stared at the wet stones that day, trying to picture the change, and now she knew exactly what to write.

But she wanted to test it, not just copy it. Theo followed her to the vegetable garden, where two rows of bean plants stood side by side. On one row, aphids clustered on the undersides of the leaves, thick as green sand. On the other row, ladybugs prowled the same leaves, and the plants looked clean. Last month, Uncle Ray had sprayed the far row and let the near one alone, and Naomi had decided back then not to intervene on either one, just to watch. The result was standing right in front of her.

She flipped her paper over and drew two arrows instead of one, from the sun to the beans to the aphids to the ladybugs, and then a heavy line through the ladybug link. She held it up so Theo could see. "This row is the shore without its starfish," she said, pointing at the crawling leaves.

Theo looked at the paper, then at the beans, and set the axe down for good. "Okay," he said. "Show me which one to draw first."

activity: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
story:
Justin spread the parts across the workbench in his grandfather's garage: marbles, wooden beads, a bag of tiny silver ball bearings, and a loop of stiff wire. The science fair was on Thursday, and his model of a helium atom had to be right.

He glued two marbles and two wooden beads together for the middle, then bent the wire into two rings around it. For the electrons he chose two more marbles, white ones, because they matched. He was reaching for the glue when his older sister Nadia came in to borrow the duct tape.

"Those are your electrons?" she said.

"Yeah, so?"

"Look it up." She tossed him her phone and took the tape.

Justin typed in the mass of a proton versus an electron. The number came back: a proton has about 1,836 times the mass of an electron. He read it twice. His white marbles were basically the same size as the marbles in the nucleus. He tried to picture what 1,836 marbles would look like, and the picture failed. The nucleus would weigh more than everything on the workbench put together.

So almost all of an atom's mass was packed into that little lump in the middle, he thought, and the electrons were almost nothing at all. His model said the opposite. He stood there holding a white marble in each hand, feeling like he'd built the whole thing backwards.

He tested it. He set one marble, for a proton, on the scale from the fishing tackle box. Then he tried to weigh a single ball bearing. The scale didn't even twitch. He added bearings one at a time, counting under his breath, and quit past fifty because his eyes were giving out and the needle had barely moved. That settled it.

He pried the marble electrons off the wire with a screwdriver and replaced them with two ball bearings, so small he had to glue them onto loops of thread to keep from losing them. The marbles and beads stayed in the nucleus, where the mass belonged. Then he made a card for the table: helium, two protons, two neutrons, two electrons, and underneath, in his most careful printing, that a proton has about 1,836 times the mass of an electron.

On Thursday a judge stopped at his table, a man with gray hair and a veteran air force jacket. He read the card, then picked up the model and turned it over in his hands.

"The kid who made this one," he said to the other judge, "actually looked it up instead of guessing." He set it down and tapped the nucleus with one finger. "Start here. Almost everything is in here."

Justin's face went hot, but not in a bad way. He glanced at the two ball bearings glinting on their threads and said, "They're the smallest parts I could find, and even they're way too big."

The judge laughed and wrote something on his clipboard.

activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
story:
Peyton stood in the doorway of Ratskeller, the German restaurant her mother had picked for her birthday dinner, and realized the plan had a flaw. Her mother had disappeared toward the back, the hostess had vanished with a tray, and Peyton had no idea where anything was. Every sign was in curly German letters she couldn't read.

It wasn't that she knew nothing. Every Tuesday in German class, Frau Bell had them play a game where one kid wore a blindfold and a partner steered them around the room using only three words. Peyton had been the guide last week, marching her blindfolded friend Maya between the desks. "Links means left," Peyton had said, turning Maya by the elbow. "Rechts means right. And geradeaus means straight ahead, so walk, don't wobble." Maya had giggled the whole way and walked straight into the recycling bin anyway. Peyton had laughed too, but the words had stuck like gum to a shoe.

Now she hovered near the kitchen, feeling like she was on a scavenger hunt with no clue sheet. A waiter rushed past carrying two enormous plates, and behind him a man with silver hair leaned toward a woman at the register and asked a question Peyton caught only pieces of: "Wo ist ... ?" The woman answered quickly, "Durch die Tür, dann links, und geradeaus." Door, then links, then geradeaus. Peyton's heart sped up. Left and straight ahead, she thought. That's the pattern. A bathroom was usually down a little hallway like that, and if the man was asking, the answer had to be directions.

She followed the silver-haired man at a distance, past the kitchen door, then watched him turn left and head straight down a narrow corridor. She counted the words against his feet. Links when he went left, geradeaus when he kept going. It matched. But at the end of the hall he didn't stop at any bathroom door. He pushed through the last door on the right, and light and music spilled out, and a dozen voices shouted something in German that ended with her mother's name.

The room was full of her mother's friends, a cake in the middle of the table big enough that a whole basketball team could consume it in one sitting. "Surprise," her mother said, switching to English and grinning. "Happy birthday, Peyton." The silver-haired man turned around, and Peyton saw he was her uncle from Hamburg, the one who always sent postcards. "You followed me," he said, raising his eyebrows. "The whole way?"

"Links, then geradeaus," Peyton said. "Though I was hoping for a bathroom."

Her uncle laughed and pointed back down the hall. "That one is rechts, first door." He held out a slice of cake taller than her hand. "But eat first. Whether it is the best cake in the family is subjective, and your grandmother has been arguing about it all afternoon."

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
story:
Sawyer discovered the pimple on Tuesday morning, right in the middle of his chin, and school photos were on Friday. He leaned close to the bathroom mirror and prodded it, which only made it redder. In the kitchen he found a note from his mom, who had already left for work: "There's five dollars on the counter. The pharmacy on Miller Street has face wash. Ask the pharmacist if you're not sure which one. Love, Mom."

At the pharmacy, Sawyer stood in the aisle reading labels, feeling like his stamina for weird grown-up words was running out fast. Salicylic acid, benzoyl peroxide, oil-free. He finally carried two bottles to the counter, where a pharmacist with reading glasses on a chain looked up from a box of prescriptions.

"First one?" she asked.

"First one," Sawyer admitted. "I don't even get where it came from. I washed my face yesterday."

"Yesterday's not the problem," she said. "During puberty, hormones tell your skin's oil glands to make more oil. That oil is called sebum, and it can clog your pores. Clogged pores cause acne."

"So it's happening under there," Sawyer said slowly, "before I can even see it."

"Exactly." She tapped the smaller bottle. "This one, once a day. Be patient."

He tested the idea like a science experiment. Each morning he washed his face and swiped on deodorant, because if puberty was making oil glands work overtime, other changes were probably happening too, and his gym teacher had made some very explicit comments about the class needing showers after practice. His armpits had their own opinions now. He kept a chart on the back of his notebook, marking the pimple's size with a pencil dot each day. Wednesday, big dot. Thursday, smaller dot. Friday morning, the dot was barely a speck.

At photo time, Sawyer stood in line and turned his chin toward the camera anyway, just slightly, the way he'd practiced. The photographer counted down. Right before the flash, the kid behind him whispered, "Nice shirt."

"Thanks," Sawyer said. "Washed my face, too."

activity: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
story:
Parker slid into the booth at the Snowcap Cafe with his notebook, two pencils, and a hot chocolate so tall it could insulate an entire village against the February tundra outside. His older sister Dana dumped her own essay onto the table and stole a marshmallow off his whipped cream.

"You're doing my least favorite thing today," she said. "Five paragraphs. Introduction, three reasons, conclusion."

"Mrs. Okafor says the introduction grabs you like a fishhook," Parker said, "and the conclusion is where you let the fish go, but in a good mood."

"That's suspiciously poetic." Dana tapped his page. "What's your topic?"

"Longer recess. Obvious choice."

He wrote his three reasons in his messiest handwriting: kids focus better, kids get more exercise, kids stop going rebellious by fourth period. Dana read over his shoulder and made a sound like a deflating balloon.

"This is fine," she said, "but it's all one-sided. Nobody who disagrees with you is going to flip sides just because you listed three things they already decided to ignore."

"Then what's the point of the whole essay?"

Dana grinned, which was never a good sign. "Here's the weird thing I learned the hard way. You have to put in the best argument against you. State it fairly, like it's actually a good point. Then answer it. That answer is called a rebuttal. My English teacher circled mine in red and wrote 'finally' next to it, which was either a compliment or an insult."

Parker frowned at his page. "So I write that teachers say recess wastes class time, and then I knock it down?"

"No knocking. Fair first, then answer."

He tested the idea right there, reading his new paragraph aloud over the hiss of the espresso machine. "Some teachers argue that longer recess takes away learning time, which matters because our school days are already short. But students who get more breaks focus better afterward, so the time we lose comes back to us doubled." He looked up. "Dana. That sounds like I know what I'm talking about."

"You kind of do. Terrifying."

Parker copied the whole paragraph into his notebook, then drew a fishhook on the introduction and a small victorious fish on the conclusion. His hot chocolate had gone lukewarm, so he wrapped both hands around it anyway.

Dana slid his notebook back across the table. "Congratulations. You now write better than half of ninth grade."

"Only half?" Parker said. "I'm aiming for at least two-thirds by Friday."

He flagged down the cashier and ordered a second hot chocolate, for research purposes, and got back to work.

activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
story:
Jessica's problem was that Mrs. Okafor had written "Is it a physical change or a chemical change?" on the board, and Jessica's reflex was to guess chemical, because chemical sounded like the fancier answer. She had guessed chemical for melting ice, chemical for tearing paper, and chemical, most extravagantly, for dissolving salt in water. Three red X's in a row.

"It's a physical change," said her lab partner, Dex, who was careful with his goggles and even more careful with his answers. "Melting, tearing, dissolving. The stuff is still the stuff."

"Salt disappears, though," Jessica said. "That's not still the stuff. That's gone."

Dex shrugged, which was his way of saying he had done the reading and she had not.

Jessica refused to lose the argument on a shrug. She got two beakers, filled them with water, and stirred a spoon of salt into each one until the grains vanished. Then she covered one beaker and set the other, uncovered, on the sunny windowsill behind the aquarium. She wrote her name on masking tape and stuck it to the glass, because someone in third period had a habit of claiming every interesting experiment as their own.

For three days she checked the window. The water level crept down. On Friday the beaker held only a damp white crust along the bottom, and when Jessica scraped it with the spoon, the crystals crumbled exactly the way salt did, sharp and gritty on her fingertip. She touched her tongue to it, just barely, and winced.

"Dex," she said, holding up the beaker. "It came back."

He leaned over. "Same salt?"

"Same salt. Evaporating the water leaves it behind." She tapped the glass. "So it's physical. The water went somewhere, but the salt never turned into anything else. It was just hiding."

Mrs. Okafor walked past, looked into the beaker, and wrote something in her binder without a word. Jessica decided that was probably a good sign.

She poured fresh water onto the crust and watched the salt slip away into it again, invisible, patient, ready to argue with her some other day.

activity: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
story:
The clock above the whiteboard showed four minutes left when Mrs. Okafor dropped the bomb. "Last problem of the day," she said. "First correct answer earns the resilient green trophy, and it stays on your desk all week."

Colton's pencil was already moving. The problem was 1/3 + 1/4, and fractions with different bottom numbers had beaten him before. In October, on a worksheet he still remembered, he had written 2/7 and handed it in feeling proud, only to find a big red circle around it. His grandfather had looked at that worksheet that night and said only, "Sevenths and thirds don't speak the same language, kiddo. Find a language they both speak." Colton had stared at the page until bedtime without finding it.

Now Marcus across the table was scribbling fast, and Priya had her hand halfway up already. Colton felt his heart hammering against his ribs like something trying to escape.

Different denominators. Same language. What language did thirds and fourths both speak? He gripped his pencil. Twelveths, a voice in his head whispered, and he almost wrote it, but he didn't know where the whisper came from, so he tested it the way his grandfather tested a fence post, by pushing.

Three times four is twelve. A third of twelve is four, so 1/3 equals 4/12. A fourth of twelve is three, so 1/4 equals 3/12. Four twelfths plus three twelfths, seven twelfths. His hand shot up so fast he knocked over his eraser.

Priya had written 7/12 too, but her scratch paper was blank. "How?" she whispered as Mrs. Okafor checked both papers.

"I multiplied the denominators," Colton whispered back, keeping his voice low so Marcus couldn't steal it. "Three times four is twelve, and twelve works for both."

"Then why is yours crossed out?" Priya pointed. Colton's paper showed 7/12, then 7/12 again in bigger print, because he had checked it twice before raising his hand.

Mrs. Okafor held up both papers. "Both correct. But Priya, show us yours." Priya stood frozen, her blank scratch paper glowing under the lights like snow on the tundra, wide and empty and offering nowhere to hide.

"He taught me," she blurted, pointing at Colton. "Just now. Multiplying the denominators always gives you a number both fractions can use."

Mrs. Okafor raised an eyebrow. "It always works," she agreed, "though you don't always get the smallest one that way. Sometimes you'll have to simplify afterward. Priya, how did you get seven twelfths with no work shown?"

The room went quiet. Priya looked at the floor, then at the poster that depicted the fraction wall, thirds in one row, fourths in the row beneath, and the two rows meeting exactly at twelve.

"I counted the bricks on the poster," she admitted.

Mrs. Okafor laughed and set the little green trophy down between them. "Then share it. Colton gets it Monday, Wednesday, and Friday."

"Deal," Colton said, and slid it across the table to Priya first.

activity: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first
story:
Aiden had exactly one week before the astronomy club's night hike, and the telescope at Hendricks' Hobby Shop was on sale for one hundred fifty dollars. He had forty-two. His mom had said something careful about money being tight this month, so Aiden went to his friend Priya, who was drawing bats on her binder.

"You could put it on your mom's credit card and pay her back later," Priya said.

"That's what I thought too," Aiden said. "Then I found her card agreement in the junk drawer, that whole contract thing they send in the envelope. It said twenty-four percent interest if you don't pay it all off."

Priya wrinkled her nose. "Twenty-four percent of what, though? That's like, twenty-four cents on a dollar. That's nothing."

Aiden had thought the same thing until Thursday, when he was killing time in the library and found a book about money with a whole chapter on debt. He read one line twice, then carried it to Priya's table and read it out loud. "It's called the rule of 72," he said. "Watch. You divide 72 by the yearly interest rate, and that's about how many years money takes to double."

Priya grabbed his pencil. "Seventy-two divided by twenty-four is..." She counted on her fingers, then wrote the number three in the margin of her notebook. "Three? So if your mom couldn't pay it off, the hundred fifty dollars would turn into about three hundred in three years?"

"That's the part I got wrong," Aiden admitted. "I thought interest just sat there. It grows." He copied the math onto his hand so he wouldn't forget it. "So the telescope costs one hundred fifty dollars, or it could cost three hundred. Saving up first is the real sale."

That night a message was taped to the fridge in his mom's handwriting. "Aiden, if you're serious about the telescope, here's my offer. I'll cover the rest, but only after you've saved your share, and only if it comes with a warranty in case you drop it off a hill. Love, Mom. P.S. Who ate the last of the cheddar? Owls are nocturnal. So, apparently, are cheese thieves."

Aiden laughed, then checked the club schedule and groaned. The night hike was Saturday. He had four days and one hundred eight dollars to go. He shoveled two driveways, sold three old graphic novels to the used bookstore, and helped Mr. Hendricks stack boxes behind the shop for ten dollars and a promise not to tell anyone he'd cried during a planetarium show in fifth grade.

On Saturday, Aiden counted out crisp bills at the register while his mom watched with her arms crossed, smiling. Mr. Hendricks slid the box across the counter, tapped the warranty card stapled to the receipt, and said, "You're the first kid all year who paid cash. What's your secret?"

Aiden hefted the box onto his shoulder. "Seventy-two divided by twenty-four."

activity: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
story:
Gavin had been sitting on the floor between the shelves of Second Story Books for forty minutes, and his worksheet still said the same thing: "Find the theme of your novel. Support it with one quotation." The novel was The Castle on Vale Street, and the quote he'd chosen was "Some families are just born bad, and nothing can change that." It felt strong. It felt like the whole point of the book. But something about it tickled at him, like a word he'd almost remembered.

Across the aisle, Priya was flipping through a nature magazine, reading about birds that migrate across whole oceans every autumn. Gavin crawled over to her and held out his worksheet. "Does this work? The theme is that some families are born bad."

Priya squinted at the quote. Then she tipped her head. "Who says it in the book?"

"The grandmother," Gavin said. "Right before she locks the gate."

Priya laughed and tossed her magazine aside. "She's the villain. She's the one the whole story is fighting against."

Gavin sat back on his heels. Was that how it worked? Could a book put a character's opinion in your mouth only to knock it down? He raced back through the chapters in his head. The grandmother said it, yes, but then Rosa spent the entire book proving the opposite, teaching her little brother to read, breaking the lock on the gate. Maybe the author had planted the grandmother's cruel idea there on purpose, the way a magician plants a card, so the ending could flip it over.

He smelled the dusty vanilla of the old shop and pulled the novel back off the shelf, hunting for Rosa's line near the end. He found it on page 198: "We are not what we inherit. We are what we do next." Hereditary bad luck, the grandmother had claimed, and Rosa had answered her anyway.

Gavin copied the new quote in his best handwriting. "So the theme is whatever the book argues for," he said slowly, "not whatever a character argues for."

"Exactly," said Priya, and pointed at his pencil. "Now underline it before you forget."

activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
story:
Emilie arranged the strawberry baskets in a neat pyramid, the way Mrs. Okafor had shown her on her first Saturday at the farm stand. It was her third weekend working the counter, and she had begun to classify the customers in her head: the ones who bought two baskets without asking the price, the ones who squeezed every basket first, and the ones who walked away slowly, glancing back as if the strawberries might call after them.

That morning Mrs. Okafor had taped a new sign to the register. "Four dollars a basket today," she said, rubbing her hands together. "The winter crop cost me double what the summer one did, so the price is double too." Emilie remembered July, when the baskets had been two dollars and the line had stretched past the honey stand, ten and twelve people deep all morning. Her instinct had been to wave customers over the moment she spotted them.

Nobody waved today. A woman in a green coat picked up a basket, turned it over, looked at the sign, and set it back down. A man asked whether the price was a mistake. By eleven o'clock the line was gone, and the pyramid of baskets stood untouched except for one lonely sale. "I was pessimistic about the whole day anyway," Mrs. Okafor said, counting the register. "I always am when I have to raise prices."

Emilie couldn't stop thinking about it. Nothing else had changed: same berries, same stand, same Saturday crowd. Only the price had moved, and the buyers had vanished. She turned the idea over while she restacked baskets, and then she had it, the shape of a rule she couldn't see but could watch working. When the price of something rises, people buy less of it, as long as nothing else changes. She wanted to test it before she trusted it.

"Can we try something for the last hour?" she asked. "Put the price back to two dollars, just to see what happens." Mrs. Okafor frowned at her, then at the full crates that would spoil unsold. "We'd lose money on every basket," she said, but she was already peeling the old sign off the register.

They taped up a new one. Emilie stood at the counter with her heart tapping, and within ten minutes a boy from her science class was buying two baskets, then the woman in the green coat came back, then a family of four. The line rebuilt itself, basket by basket, stretching toward the honey stand just like July. Mrs. Okafor watched from behind the register, arms folded, saying nothing, and Emilie slid the last crate forward to face the crowd.

"Funny thing," Mrs. Okafor said at closing, counting a register that was fuller than the morning's. "In summer I sell cheap and sell out. In winter I sell dear and sit here all day." She held up a worn dollar bill. "Same rule both ways, isn't it?"

"That's the whole thing," Emilie said, snapping the lid on the empty crate. "Price goes up, buying goes down. Price goes down, and look at that line."

Mrs. Okafor laughed and dropped the bill into the drawer. "Then you'd better be here next Saturday."

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
story:
Emily stood in the steamy bathroom, holding the deodorant stick like evidence in a case she was trying to solve. Three days ago her older brother, Josh, had walked past her room, wrinkled his nose, and said, "Shower much?" She had thrown a sock at him, but later, in the dark, she had sniffed her own armpit and understood he wasn't just being a jerk. Something had changed, and she wanted to know what, and whether she could do anything about it.

She remembered the appointment last spring, when Josh had asked Dr. Patel the question straight out: "What actually tells the body it's time for puberty?" Emily had braced for a lecture, but the doctor had just said, "The pituitary gland in the brain signals the ovaries or testes to make more estrogen or testosterone." That was it. Josh had nodded like it was obvious, but Emily had chewed on it for weeks. A tiny gland, sending a chemical message. Nobody could see it happen. You could only see the results, the same way you couldn't see the rain coming but could watch the gutters fill.

So the smell wasn't a personal failure, she reasoned. It was a message from her own brain, and sweat glands reacting to it, and bacteria having a party in a warm damp armpit. That was the hidden cause, and hidden causes could still be interrupted. She had a simple idea to test: if she showered every morning and used deodorant right after drying off, before the bacteria could settle in, would the smell stay gone?

Her plan had two components, the daily shower and the deodorant, and she'd taped a checklist inside the medicine cabinet to keep herself honest. Day one had been easy because it was new. Day two, she'd almost skipped it, wanting ten more minutes of sleep, and had regretted that choice by lunch when she caught herself keeping her arms clamped to her sides in science class. Maybe she should have just gotten up. Maybe it didn't matter that much. She still wasn't sure.

Today was day three. She turned off the water, dried off, and swept the deodorant on before her skin had even finished cooling. The clean scent rose up sharp and minty through the steam. She pulled on her shirt, sniffed the collar once, and flipped the checklist to mark the square. From the hallway, Josh banged on the door. "You alive in there?"

"Busy," Emily called back. "Science experiment."

story:
Nicolas raised his hand in health class so fast his chair squeaked. "Question. Why do we suddenly smell? Like, what actually happens?"

Ms. Reyes pointed at the diagram on the board. "Sweat glands switch on during puberty. Sweat itself doesn't smell much, but bacteria on your skin eat it, and that's what smells."

"Bacteria," Nicolas repeated. "So the smell is basically bacteria leftovers."

"Basically, yes."

"Then the principle is simple. Kill the bacteria, or wash them off, every day. Showers and deodorant." He said it like he'd discovered electricity.

Behind him, Marcus muttered, "We know, dude. We've been using deodorant since September."

"Have you, though," said Priya, waving a hand in front of her nose. "Because there's an objective way to test it. I can smell you from here."

The class laughed. Marcus turned pink. "Okay, fine, I keep forgetting it. My brother says I don't need it yet."

That afternoon, Nicolas sat in Dr. Okafor's office for his sports physical. He'd been thinking about Marcus all day, and about himself, because his own voice had done a weird squeak during announcements that morning. "Can I ask something off topic?" he said. "Marcus thinks nothing's happening to him yet, so he doesn't need deodorant. And I'm the shortest kid in class and nothing's happening to me either. Is that normal, or are we broken?"

Dr. Okafor shook her head. "Puberty usually begins between ages 8 and 13 in girls and between 9 and 14 in boys, and starting anywhere in that range is normal. You're eleven. You've got time."

"So some kids start at nine, some at fourteen, and it's all fine?"

"All fine."

Nicolas walked back to school to meet Marcus, who was waiting by the gym doors. "Good news," Nicolas said. "We're not broken. You could start at nine or all the way at fourteen, still normal."

"Cool," said Marcus. "So I don't need deodorant."

"No. The bacteria don't care about your schedule." Nicolas pulled a stick of deodorant out of his backpack and held it out like a trophy. "Stolen from my dad's drawer. It's yours. I'm enforcing the principle."

Marcus sniffed it, shrugged, and swiped it on right there on the gym steps.

activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
story:
At Sunday dinner Adam could hardly sit still, because he had a message on his phone and he was dying to tell everyone. His cousin Marcus had texted him: "You won't believe it. Two kids at my party fought over the last piece of cake, and their dad just cut it himself and both kids screamed. How do you split cake without a war?" Adam had pushed his mashed potatoes around his plate all through dinner, thinking about it, and now he set down his fork.

"Marcus needs help," he announced. "Two kids fighting over cake. If you just cut it, someone always yells that the pieces aren't even." His dad started to say something, but Adam held up a hand. "Wait. I have an idea." He grabbed the leftover garlic bread, tore off a chunk, and put it in the middle of the table. "Okay, Dad, you and me. You split this into two parts, and I pick first." His dad cut it, eyeing the knife carefully, and Adam grabbed the bigger piece immediately. His dad groaned. They tried it again with Adam as the cutter, and this time he measured and turned the bread, slowing down, until the two parts looked exactly alike, because if he didn't, his dad would grab the better one.

"It's called divide and choose," Adam said, bouncing in his chair. "One person splits, the other picks first." His little sister demanded a turn, so he halved a dinner roll for her and she studied both halves like a judge before choosing. She pronounced them fair. Adam summarized the whole thing in a text back to Marcus: "Don't cut the cake. Let one kid divide it and the other kid picks first. Divider makes it equal or loses out."

"Smart," his mom said, collecting plates. "Your grandfather settled fights that way for years. That man ran this family like a dynasty, and that was his only rule that never failed."

"It's not arbitrary," Adam said, typing fast. "It actually works."

Then he hit send and ran for the phone to call Marcus.

activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
story:
Alex had one job at the Saturday community kitchen: bake the blueberry muffins all by himself, start to finish, while his grandmother ran the front table. The recipe card sat propped against the flour canister, soft from years of use. He measured, he cracked eggs, he folded berries in with a gentle wrist. Then he read the first line again. "Preheat oven to 375 degrees." He glanced at the clock. The lunch rush started in fifty minutes, and the oven took forever to heat up. Nobody would know if the muffins went in while the oven was still cold. They would just bake and heat at the same time, and he would save ten whole minutes.

He slid the tray in and pressed the button. Ten minutes later, the kitchen smelled right. Twenty minutes later, he pulled the tray out, and something was off. The muffins were pale on top, flat, and dense in the middle, nothing like the golden domes his grandmother made. "Huh," Alex said to the empty kitchen. He turned a muffin over and studied the pale bottom.

His friend Marisol came through the swinging door carrying an empty bread basket. "Whoa. What happened to those?" She picked one up and squished it gently. "These look sad." Alex explained that he had put them in before the oven finished heating, to save time. Marisol raised an eyebrow, her skepticism plain on her face. "My mom calls that skipping preheating," she said. "The batter has to go in only after the oven has reached the set temperature, so baking starts at the right heat." She shrugged. "That's all I know, but she says it like it's a law."

Alex looked at the recipe card, then at the wall clock, then at his flat muffins. Maybe the oven's slowness at the start had changed how they baked, even though the heat eventually arrived. He had a test for that idea. He still had enough batter for a second batch, and this time he would follow the first line exactly, no shortcuts, and see if the results came out distinct from the first batch or exactly the same. If they were the same, Marisol's mom's law was wrong. If they were different, he had found the problem.

He set the oven, and while it climbed toward 375 he washed the mixing bowl and lined the second tray with paper cups. The little indicator light glowed until, with a soft click, it went out. Alex opened the door and felt the wave of heat roll over his wrists. He slid the tray in and set the timer.

Twenty minutes later the muffins stood tall and golden. Marisol came back for the bread basket and stopped in the doorway. "Now those are muffins." She stacked two on a napkin for the front table and handed one to Alex, still warm. He took a bite, and before he could say anything, she said, "I'm officially boycotting the flat ones."

story:
The geology hall had a contest table set up beside the gift shop, and Landon spotted the sign right away. Sort twelve mystery rocks into igneous, sedimentary, or metamorphic before the three o'clock buzzer, and your name went into a drawing for a summer science scholarship to the museum's day camp. It was 2:37. His cousin Maya grabbed his sleeve. "We can do this. You're the one who reads all those rock books."

Landon picked up the first rock, dark and speckled, and dropped it into the igneous bin. "Cooled from melt," he said. "The speckles give it away." The second one had stripes, like somebody had folded chocolate into vanilla dough, and he hesitated. Heat and pressure did that, so it went to metamorphic. Muhammad stood at home plate gripping a bat he wasn't going to swing, because today the diamond was his pretend pool. His swim test was on Saturday, twenty-five metres of front crawl with side breathing, and every time he took a breath in the real pool he lifted his whole face out of the water, splashed, and stalled. His best friend Danilo sat cross-legged on the pitcher's mound, watching him pivot his head side to side.

"Slower," Danilo said. "You look like you're checking for rain."

Muhammad stopped and thought about the fastest kid in their lane, a boy named Sam who swam like a motorboat. Yesterday, from the bench, Muhammad had noticed something odd. Every time Sam breathed, half of his face seemed to stay down. One goggle lens stayed under the water while the other popped up, and he turned only far enough for his mouth to clear the surface. Muhammad had been hoisting his whole face to the sky, and every single breath cost him speed. He cherished that observation, because it was the first clue he'd found in three weeks of sinking.

"Okay, new idea," Muhammad said. He dropped the bat, lay down in the dusty infield grass, and paddled his arms in slow motion. "My left goggle stays in the water. Danilo counted for him, calling out strokes from the mound, and on the fifth breath Muhammad's roll was smooth enough that Danilo clapped. "That looked spontaneous," he said, "like you weren't even thinking about it."

"That's the whole point," Muhammad said, breathing again, faster now, arms wheeling through the dust. The team had a hierarchy for the Saturday lanes, slowest swimmers in lane one, and Muhammad was tired of lane one. He rolled, breathed with one goggle up, dropped his face, and kept his windmill arms turning all the way to the make-believe wall at second base.

On Saturday morning, Muhammad pushed off and counted his strokes, and at the first breath he kept his left lens in the water, turned only far enough for his mouth to clear the surface, and felt himself keep moving. When he slapped the far wall, Danilo was leaning over the lane rope, holding up two fingers.

"Lane two," Danilo shouted. "I heard Coach say it."

Colton had one job at the town hall meeting: narrate the slide show while his class presented their project on how laws get made. His classmate Priya leaned over and whispered, "You're missing a whole house. Federal bills have to pass the House of Commons and then the Senate."

Colton stared at his slide. His bill was only climbing one staircase. He thought about the provincial bill they had read about in the paper, the one about bike helmets. Colton took it in both hands.

story:
Noemie's book club met Saturday morning, which gave her exactly one evening to figure out what she wanted to say about The Great Gatsby. Her mother had promised she could stay up until ten, and the kitchen clock already said 7:42. She spread the library's battered copy across the table, next to a bowl of pretzels she was eating more out of stress than hunger.

The problem was Ms. Okafor's assignment: track one symbol across the whole novel and explain how its meaning changes from chapter to chapter. A symbol, Noemie had decided by dinnertime, was the sneakiest thing in fiction. It looked like an object, but it was secretly carrying ideas around, the way her landlord carried a clipboard that seemed to convey the message "I can raise the rent whenever I want." Objects that meant things. Fine. But which object, and what did it mean, and when?

She flipped back to chapter one, and there it was. On the very first night of the story, someone in her book club had noticed, Gatsby stands in his yard reaching his arms out toward the water. Noemie reread the page, and her pencil stopped. A green light glows at the end of Daisy Buchanan's dock, across the water from Gatsby's house. Gatsby is reaching toward it. "Okay," she said to the pretzel bowl. "That's the symbol."

Now she needed the change. She made three columns on a sticky note: chapter one, chapter five, chapter nine. In chapter one, Gatsby stretches toward the light like it's something he can grab. She wrote "wanting." In chapter five, she found the scene where he shows Daisy the green light from his own yard, and it suddenly seemed smaller, almost ordinary, like a firefly that had gone extinct somewhere between chapters. She wrote "having, sort of." Then chapter nine gave her the line about the green light, the enormous thing Gatsby had yearned for, and she sat back. The light hadn't moved. The dock hadn't moved. Gatsby's whole life had moved around it, and that was the trick. She wrote "too big to hold," underlined it twice, and looked up at the clock. 9:51. Nine minutes to spare.

At book club the next morning, Marcus went first and talked about cars for six straight minutes. When Noemie's turn came, she held up her sticky note, which had lost a corner to the pretzel bowl. "It's the green light at Daisy's dock," she said. "Same light every time. It's the guy looking at it who changes."

Ms. Okafor tapped her pencil once against her chair. "And in the last chapter?"

"It outgrew him," Noemie said, "or he outgrew his own idea of it." Marcus, who had not read the last chapter, quietly turned to the back of his book and started skimming.

activity: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first
story:
Clara pressed her nose against the glass case outside the school library, where a purple mountain bike sat on a folded towel with a price tag that read one hundred eighty dollars. She had counted her savings twice last night: forty-one dollars and some coins. Her mother had said, maybe for your birthday, but her birthday was in March, and the trails behind the school turned golden in October.

At dinner, her uncle Ray was squinting at a piece of paper and shaking his head. "Every month I send them money," he muttered, "and this bill barely shrinks. It's like pouring water into a bucket with a hole in it."

Clara slid into the chair across from him. "How much do you send?"

"Twenty-five dollars. That's the minimum they ask for." He tapped the paper. "But most of it, they keep. It's interest, and it's been years now."

Clara frowned. That didn't seem possible. Twenty-five dollars a month, month after month, and the number hardly went down? She took the bill to the kitchen table and did what her math teacher called a test: she circled every payment on the page, then beside each one she wrote the amount the balance had dropped. Eleven dollars. Nine dollars. Ten and a half. The rest of every payment was going somewhere she couldn't see, month after month, so the paying off just kept stretching out longer and longer, like taffy.

"Uncle Ray," she said slowly, "if you paid more than the minimum, would it end sooner?"

He rubbed his chin. "Wouldn't it be the same either way? Twenty-five is twenty-five."

She slid her paper toward him. He looked at her circles, then at the bill, then at her again. "Huh," he said. "All those years, I could have been done by now." He laughed, a short surprised sound, and folded the bill into his pocket like it was something new.

The next morning Clara stood at the case again. Eighty dollars meant waiting, and waiting was a real cost too, she could feel that. But the probability of the bike still sitting there in October seemed better than the probability of her uncle's bill ever disappearing at twenty-five dollars a month. She could ride the trails this fall owing nothing to anyone, or she could have the bike now and a shadow trailing behind it for years.

A sixth grader wandered up beside her and pointed at the price tag. "My dad just puts stuff like that on a card," he said.

Clara looked at the purple frame, the clean silver spokes, and thought of her uncle's bill, going on and on. "You know," she said, "the minimum payment is a trap. I'd save up first."

Eli crouched at the edge of the pond with his notebook, trying to draw a food chain for science homework. Sun, then algae, then a mayfly larva, then a frog, then a heron. He kept messing up the heron's beak so it looked like a shovel, like the bird planned to excavate the whole pond.

His little sister Josie plopped down beside him, chewing a granola bar. "That's not a heron. That's a pickle with legs."

"It's a top predator. Eat your snack." Eli frowned at the page. The assignment had a trick question at the bottom: what happens if one link disappears? He'd written "the frog goes hungry," but that felt too small, like saying a bridge falls down because one person trips.

"Every food chain starts with the sun," Josie said, reading over his shoulder. "We learned that in third grade."

"Obviously," said Eli. Then he stopped. Had he actually checked? He tested it right there on the bank, tracing his chain backward: heron, frog, larva, algae, sun. Worked. But was it a rule for everywhere, or just here?

"Except the dark ocean," said Josie, waving her granola bar. "We watched a movie about it. In 1977, scientists in a submarine called Alvin went down and found whole communities of animals living around deep-sea vents, pitch black, no sun ever. Totally radical."

"Submarine?"

"Submersible. Alvin. 1977. It was in the movie, I remember everything." She tapped her temple. "The food chains down there start with bacteria that use chemicals from the vents. Chemicals, not sunlight."

Eli sat back. The willow canopy dappled the water where his algae floated, sun-fed and green. Miles below some ocean, bacteria ran a whole neighborhood on vent chemicals instead. So his chain wasn't a universal law, just a local one, which felt both annoying and excellent, like finding a secret door in his own house.

He wrote his answer: here, remove the algae and the frog, the heron, everything above it collapses, because at this pond the sun is the bottom link. Then he drew a tiny Alvin at the corner of the page, just to show the teacher he knew about the exception.

"For the pickle heron," Josie said, "you should draw it eating a sea pickle."

"Sea pickles are real, Josie."

"Then draw two."

"Read it before you laugh," Marcus said.

"Friendship," Marcus said. "That's obviously it. The two main characters are friends, they fight, they make up, done."

"Then why do I feel like we're missing something?" Emily pulled out her battered copy of the novel and flipped to the scene where Jax lends Devon his lucky paddle. Marcus leaned over. "So friendship isn't just the answer. It's like the topic."

Emily grabbed the pen off his ear, where he kept it like a tiny hierarchy of pens, the blue one always on top. She wrote on the back of Priya's note: "A topic is a subject a novel is about. Tomorrow at lunch, Emily was going to read that quotation out loud and watch Priya's face. She practiced the words one more time under her breath as the bus pulled up to the school.

story:
Savannah stood in the empty community theatre with her script rolled in one fist, waiting for Mrs. Okafor's verdict. She had performed her monologue three times, and three times the director had said the same thing: "It's all one speed, Savannah. Where do you stop to think?" Savannah wanted the role of the lighthouse keeper more than she had wanted anything since the summer her family almost moved away, and she could not figure out what she was doing wrong. The words were right. The feelings were right. Something invisible was missing.

In the third row, chewing a straw, sat Marcus, the eighth grader who had been in eleven plays. He flipped through his own script, and Savannah noticed something she had never seen before: pencil slashes cut across the pages, a dozen on some pages, like little fences between the lines. "What are those?" she asked. Marcus shrugged. "Beats. A new beat starts wherever the character's thought or tactic changes. The pause is where you switch." Savannah frowned. "But a pause is just... nothing. Empty air." Marcus grinned. "That's what everyone thinks at first."

She took her script to the lobby and read it like a detective. The lighthouse keeper begins by begging the storm to spare her sister's boat. Then, halfway down the page, the keeper stops begging and starts bargaining, offering herself instead. Savannah read the speech aloud in a whisper and found it: the thought changed right after the line "Take me instead of her." She drew a slash there, and two more, one for every place the keeper's mind turned. Then she abandoned her old plan of rushing through the whole speech before she lost her nerve, because now she could see the speech had doors in it, and she was allowed to stand in each doorway.

The twist came at the next rehearsal. Savannah paused after "Take me instead of her," and Mrs. Okafor called out, "Perfect. That's exactly the beat." But when she paused again after "I have kept this light for thirty years," the director tilted her head. "Why are you stopping there?" Savannah froze. She had marked it because it sounded like a big line, but the keeper's thought hadn't actually changed there; she was still bargaining, just louder. "I don't know," Savannah admitted. "I think I put a slash where it just felt dramatic." Mrs. Okafor laughed. "Then erase it. A pause without a reason is just dead air."

Savannah erased the slash, and the monologue snapped together like a lock. In the performance, when she reached the bargaining line, she let the silence stretch until she could hear someone in the second row hold their breath, and only then did she say, "Take me instead of her." Afterward Marcus found her by the snack table, where they split a stale pretzel like it was a treaty ending a long war. "You paused forever," he said. "I thought you forgot the line." "No," Savannah said, and held up her script, slashes showing faint through the stage lights' glow. "I was just changing my mind."

Emilie slid the last flat of strawberries across the counter at Mateo's berry stand, where she worked every Saturday morning for four dollars an hour. The sign made her stop. Last week the berries were three dollars a basket. Today it said five. "Mateo, did someone make a mistake?"

He shook his head and pointed toward the hills, where the fields flourished in rows all summer. "Frost on Tuesday night. Took out half the crop." He lifted a basket so she could see it. "These are what's left."

Emilie took a breath. "There was a frost. It ruined half the crop, so there aren't as many berries, and the ones that are left cost more."

The woman looked at the baskets, then at her kids' faces, and bought two anyway. "Good explanation," she said, counting out the bills.

Emilie wrote FROST on the little chalkboard by the register, so the next customer wouldn't have to ask. Mateo grinned and slipped an extra basket into her tote at closing time. "For the telescope fund," he said.

story:
Quinn slid her math notebook across the counter of her grandfather's corner store, between the register and a rack of gum. The last customer of the afternoon had just left, and the only sounds were the hum of the drink cooler and rain ticking on the front window. "Grandpa, before you check it," she said, "I want to check it myself. But I don't know how."

Her grandfather was meticulous about homework; he read every page with a pencil in his hand and circled anything that looked off. Last week he had circled three problems, and the guilt Quinn felt about those three circles had kept her up past bedtime. This week's page was two-step equations, and below them, a small coordinate grid where she was supposed to plot the line y equals 3x plus 4.

"Well," he said, peeling an orange, "you solved for x in the first three. What did you get?"

"For the first one, x equals 5. The equation was 3x plus 4 equals 19." She said it fast, the way you say something you're not sure of.

"Here's a trick my teacher taught me, back when the store was just a fruit cart," he said. "Take your answer and put it back in place of x. If both sides come out equal, the answer is right."

Quinn frowned at her notebook. "Put it back in? Like... I solved to get rid of it, and now I put it back?"

"That's the whole trick. Try it out loud."

"Three times 5 is 15. Then 15 plus 4 is 19." She paused. "And the other side already says 19. They're both 19." She looked up. "So it's right? Both sides came out equal, so it's right?"

"You tell me."

She tried the second one, 2x minus 7 equals 9, with her answer of 8. Two times 8 was 16, minus 7 was 9, and the other side was 9. Equal again. Her spine straightened a little. But the third one, 4x plus 5 equals 17, with her answer of 3, gave her trouble: 4 times 3 was 12, plus 5 was 17. Equal. That was right too. Then why had she felt so unsure?

The fourth one stopped her cold. 5x minus 6 equals 14, and she had written x equals 2. Five times 2 was 10, minus 6 was 4. The other side said 14. Four did not equal fourteen. Her pencil hovered. Somewhere she had gone wrong. She redid the steps slowly, adding 6 to both sides to get 5x equals 20, and then dividing, which gave x equals 4. She put 4 back in place of the variable: 20 minus 6 was 14, and the other side was 14. Equal. "It's 4," she said, crossing out the 2. "The old answer failed the check."

Then she turned to the grid. If y equaled 3x plus 4, she could pick x, work out y, and plot the point. She tried x equals 0, which made y equal 4, and marked the point. Then x equals 1 gave y equals 7, so up went a second point. She drew a line through them and noticed it climbed three squares for every one across, just like the 3 in the equation. On a hunch she checked her line against the equation: the point where x was 1 should sit at y equals 7, and 3 times 1 plus 4 made 7. Equal. The line and the equation agreed with each other.

Her grandfather set a peeled orange slice on the corner of her notebook, right beside the grid. "So it's a picture," she said, tapping the sloping line. "The equation and the graph both depict the same thing, just different ways."

"Good as any poster in here," he said, and turned the sign on the door to CLOSED.
