activity: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
story:
Eli stood at the shallow end of the community pool, gripping the gutter with both hands, watching the lane ropes bob like green snakes. Twenty-five metres. That was the whole test: one length of front crawl, breathing to the side whenever he wanted. His problem was that whenever he turned his head, water went straight up his nose, and he had to stop, coughing, while the other kids in Level Four swam on without him.

"You're almost there," said Priya from the next lane, treading water. "You've got the arms."

"It's the breathing," Eli said. "If I lift my head up to get air, my legs sink. If I keep my head down, I drink half the pool."

Priya laughed, then stopped, because she could see he wasn't. "Want me to watch you do one length and see what happens?"

He pushed off and swam. Three strokes, then a fourth, and on the fourth he twisted his whole face up toward the ceiling, gasped, got a mouthful of chlorine, and stood up coughing. His eyes stung. The water's smell hung around him like something corrosive, sharp enough that he could almost feel it eating at his good mood. He wiped his face on his shoulder and thought hard.

Here was the strange part. When he'd watched his friend Marcus swim, Marcus barely seemed to turn his head at all. His cheek just touched the water and somehow he got air. Eli had also noticed something in his own swimming, though he'd never thought about it until now: when he blew out underwater, little bubbles rushed past his ear, and there seemed to be a small pocket of air, a little dip in the water, right beside his face. His own head, plowing forward, was pushing a bow wave, and that wave left a lower spot next to his cheek. The water there sat below the level of the flat surface. Which meant his mouth didn't have to reach up to the flat water at all. The air was already down there, waiting beside him, like a moon keeping a tiny orbit around his head.

"Watch this," he said to Priya. "I'm going to try keeping one goggle in the water and one eye out."

He pushed off again. Stroke, stroke, stroke, and then, instead of lifting, he just rolled his head, keeping his cheek low, letting his mouth hang in that little dip. Air. Clean, cold, real air, without his legs dropping like stones. He blew bubbles underwater, rolled again, breathed again, and kept going, all the way to the far wall, where he grabbed the gutter, gasping and grinning.

"Twenty-five metres!" Priya shouted from three lanes over. "I counted!"

Eli looked back down the lane at the water he'd crossed. Somewhere out there, microbes too small to see were probably having a fine afternoon, and he had just out-swum every single one of them.

"Same time tomorrow?" Priya called as she climbed out.

"Tomorrow I try fifty," Eli said, and shook the water from his hair like a dog.

story:
Victor sat at his grandpa's kitchen table with a pencil, an eraser, and a stubborn problem: the art club needed a shaded sphere by Friday, and his looked like a flat grey cookie. He had filled in the whole dark side with the same even grey, exactly like the handout said, and somehow it had come out worse than a blank circle.

He grabbed an orange from the fruit bowl and held it under the lamp. Maybe drawing from life instead of memory would nurture a better result than guessing had. He squinted at the dark side. "Huh," he said out loud. "It's not the same grey all over."

His grandpa shuffled in, sneezing twice. "That cat of yours. I swear I've developed an allergy to her since you brought her for the visit." He set down his tea and looked over Victor's shoulder. "Don't ask me. I can't draw a straight fence post."

"I wasn't going to ask," Victor said, though he had been about to. He turned the orange slowly. The brightest spot sat right where the lamp hit it. Then came a curving edge where light gave up, and just past that edge, on the side away from the lamp, ran the darkest band of all. Farther around, near the far edge, the grey actually got lighter again, like something was faintly glowing back into it.

Victor leaned close, testing his idea with the pencil tip hovering over his paper. He shaded his sphere's dark side in bands: light near the far edge, and darkest in one curved stripe just past where the light stopped. "The darkest band on the ball itself," he murmured, drawing it in. He tapped the stripe. "It's not the edge of the shadow. It's just past it."

The cat leapt onto the table and batted the orange, and it rolled right off the edge and under the radiator. Victor stared at his finished drawing, a real sphere now, round and solid on the flat page, and laughed. "Fine. You can keep the model."
